newsitem.title: USA: Massachusetts seeks limit on teen acesss to tobacco.
newsitem.headline: Massachusetts seeks limit on teen acesss to tobacco.

text.p: Two Massachusetts legislators introduced measures on Thursday that would require tobacco retailers to be licensed, demand photo identification as proof of age and keep cigarettes locked up or behind the counter.

Despite the state's law banning sales of tobacco products to those under the age of 18, "kids in Massachusetts smoked five million packs of cigarettes" annually, State Sen. Warren Tolman, D-Watertown, told reporters at a state house news conference.
"Kids are buying cigarettes illegally in gas stations, convenience stores, supermarkets and liquor stores across our Commonwealth and it has got to stop," he said.

Flanked by sculptures of the Eiffel Tower and a cruise ship made with cigarettes confiscated from teenagers who illegally bought them, Tolman said the centerpiece of the legislation was requiring all tobacco retailers to obtain a permit from the local board of health to sell the products.
A similar measure introduced by State Rep. Jim Marzilli, D- Arlington in the state House of Representatives, would also require tobacco to be sold from behind the counter or from a locked case.
The new Massachusetts measures would give the state an enforcement mechanism for Food and Drug Administration regulations barring tobacco's sale to minors that are slated to go into effect on Friday.

Massachusetts is battling the tobacco companies in several court cases. Like 21 other states, it is seeking to recoup Medicare costs from the industry and, separately, is attempting to have the tobacco companies list the ingredients by weight or measure in each brand of cigarettes and smokless tobacco.
Tobacco industry representatives, who are expected to oppose the measure, could not be reached for immediate comment.
